ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The Eastern Southern Alps are the eastern portion of the late Cretaceous-Quaternary S-verging back-thrust belt of the Alpine chain, bounded to the north by the Insubric-Periadriatic line (Doglioni and Bosellini, 1987; Castellarin and Cantelli, 2000). The outer thrust front is composed by NE-SW to E-W trending faults and folds emerging along the mountain front or buried below the Quaternary foredeep and continental sediments of the Veneto-Friuli plain (Galadini et al., 2005), which were used to define the Neogene-Quaternary timing of activity of these structures (Caputo et al., 2010). To the east the Southalpine thrusts interact with the NW-SE trending, dextral strike-slip faults of the Idrija fault system in the Slovenia border region (Bajc et al., 2001; Burrato et al., 2008; Kastelic et al., 2008). Similar structural setting can be deduced for the more northern parts of the South Alpine unit, where the south vergent thrusts of the Friulain Alps and Pre-alps interact with the strike-slip extrusion structure of the Periadriatic fault system.
The Jesenice seismogenic source represents the seismogenic portion of the NWW-SEE to NW-SE oriented Sava active fault located in the Upper Sava valley and bounded to the west by the Tarvisio seismogenic source, which seems to be the continuation of the seismogenic process in the more western portion along the southern margin of the Periadriatic fault zone. The minimum and maximum depth were inferred from geologic and regional structural setting (Placer, 2008; Zivcic et al., 2011; Reinecker and Lenhardt, 1999). The strike is based on geologic and geomorphological maps and data (Vrabec, 2001; Kastelic, 2007; Placer, 2008; Jamsek Rupnik, 2013), while the dip of the source was inferred from geological and geomorphological observations. The rake was inferred from structural (Vrabec, 2001; Kastelic, 2007; Jamsek Rupnik, 2013) and earthquake data (focal mechanisms and horizontal maximum stress orientations combined with the geometry of the source) (Zivcic et al., 2011; Reinecker and Lenhardt, 1999). The slip rate was inferred considering finite element modeling and geodynamic considerations as the long-term seismogenic slip rates (Kastelic and Carafa, 2012). Slip rates higher than the reported values are calculated from surface geologic data (Jamsek Rupnik, 2013) and regional estimations from GPS data (Vrabec and Fodor, 2006) but are considered to be the cumulative deformation rates. The maximum magnitude was inferred from fault geometry and from geophysical and seismological considerations.
